prompt: A lecture room measures $4.0\ \mathrm m\times5.0\ \mathrm m\times2.5\ \mathrm m$. Air density is $1.20\ \mathrm{g/L}$. Find the mass of air in the room, in kg.
solution:
Volume: $4.0\times5.0\times2.5=50\ \mathrm m^3$ (units).
$1\ \mathrm{g/L}=\dfrac{10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kg}}{10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^3}}=1\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$ (units: both prefixes cancel).
Mass $=1.20\times50=60\ \mathrm{kg}$ (dimanal check: $\mathrm{kg/m^3}\cdot\mathrm{m^3}=\mathrm{kg}$).
Trap: reading $1\ \mathrm{g/L}$ as $1000\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$ gives $6\times10^4$ kg.
hints: Convert density to kg/m³ before multiplying.

prompt: A pressure of $3.0\ \mathrm{kPa}$ is expressed in CGS units, $\mathrm{g\,cm^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$. Its value is

why: converted metres to centimetres but forgot kg to g
converted kg to g and kPa to Pa but forgot the length conversion
inverted the length conversion: used $1\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}=100\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$
treated Pa as already CGS and only converted kPa to Pa

rubric.text: Each base unit converted with the right power of ten and direction
Final power of ten checked against $1\ \mathrm{Pa}=10\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$

solution:
$1\ \mathrm{Pa}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$ (dimanal: $\mathrm N/\mathrm m^2$).
$1\ \mathrm{kg}=10^{3}\ \mathrm g$ gives a factor $10^{3}$.
$1\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}=10^{-2}\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ gives a factor $10^{-2}$ (units: a longer unit makes the number smaller).
$1\ \mathrm{Pa}=10\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$, so $3.0\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{Pa}\to3.0\times10^{4}$.
hints: Pa = kg m⁻¹ s⁻²; convert each base unit separately.

prompt: A pendulum of length $L=1.000\pm0.002\ \mathrm m$ has period $T=2.007\pm0.004\ \mathrm s$. Use $g=4\pi^{2}L/T^{2}$. Treat the errors as independent and add relative errors in quadrature. Find the uncertainty $\delta g$ in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

rubric.text: Power rule: $T^{-2}$ doubles the relative error of $T$

solution:
$g=4\pi^2(1.000)/2.007^2\approx9.80\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ (sigfig: keep 3-4 figures).
$\delta L/L=0.002$; $T$ enters squared, so its contribution is $2\,\delta T/T=2(0.004/2.007)=0.00399$ (scaling: power rule).
Quadrature: $\delta g/g=\sqrt{0.002^2+0.00399^2}\approx0.00446$.
$\delta g\approx9.80\times0.00446\approx0.044\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$.
Trap: linear addition gives $0.059$.
hints: Relative error of $T^2$ is twice that of $T$.

prompt: A resistance is found as $R=V/I$ with $V=12.0\pm0.6\ \mathrm V$ and $I=2.00\pm0.10\ \mathrm A$. The errors are independent. The percentage uncertainty in $R$ is

why: added the percent errors linearly
kept only one of the two equal contributions
summed the squared fractions but forgot the square root
treated a quotient as a difference of percent errors

rubric.text: Quotient handled by adding, not subtracting, the contributions

solution:
$\delta V/V=0.6/12.0=5.0\%$; $\delta I/I=0.10/2.00=5.0\%$ (sigfig: fractional errors).
For a quotient, relative errors add in quadrature, never cancel (error propagation).
$\delta R/R=\sqrt{0.05^2+0.05^2}=0.0707$, so $7.1\%$ (units: $R=6.0\ \Omega$).
Linear sum $10\%$ is an upper bound for correlated errors only.
hints: Divide each absolute error by its value first.

prompt: The speed $v$ of a deep-water surface wave depends only on its wavelength $\lambda$, the gravitational acceleration $g$ and the water density $\rho$. Dimensional analysis shows $v$ is proportional to

why: gets units of 1/s, not m/s
has units $\mathrm{m^2/s^2}$, the square of a speed
leaves a stray $\mathrm{kg/m^3}$ that nothing can cancel
leaves a stray $\mathrm{kg/m^3}$ under the root

rubric.text: Mass argument: $\rho$ is the only mass-carrying quantity, so it cannot appear
Exponents of $g$ and $\lambda$ solved from length and time

solution:
$[v]=\mathrm{L\,T^{-1}}$, $[\lambda]=\mathrm L$, $[g]=\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}$, $[\rho]=\mathrm{M\,L^{-3}}$ (dimanal).
Only $\rho$ contains $\mathrm M$, so its exponent must be $0$.
Take $v\propto g^a\lambda^b$: time gives $-2a=-1$, so $a=\tfrac12$ (units: seconds).
Length gives $a+b=1$, so $b=\tfrac12$ (scaling: $v\propto\sqrt{\lambda}$).
Result: $v\propto\sqrt{g\lambda}$.
hints: Mass appears in only one variable.

prompt: The period $T$ of small oscillations of a liquid drop depends only on its density $\rho$, radius $R$ and surface tension $\sigma$ (units $\mathrm{N/m}$). A drop of radius $2.0\ \mathrm{mm}$ oscillates with $T=8.0\ \mathrm{ms}$. For the same liquid, find $T$ in ms for a drop of radius $3.0\ \mathrm{mm}$.

rubric.text: Dimensional combination of $\rho,R,\sigma$ with units of time found
Scaling ratio applied to the measured $T$

solution:
$[\sigma]=\mathrm{kg\,s^{-2}}$, $[\rho]=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $[R]=\mathrm m$ (units).
$\rho R^3/\sigma$ has units $\mathrm{kg}\cdot\mathrm{s^2/kg}=\mathrm{s^2}$ (dimanal).
So $T\propto\sqrt{\rho R^3/\sigma}\propto R^{3/2}$ at fixed liquid.
$T=8.0\times(3.0/2.0)^{3/2}=8.0\times1.837=14.7\ \mathrm{ms}$ (scaling).
Trap: $T\propto R$ gives $12$; $T\propto R^{2}$ gives $18$.
hints: Find the combination of rho, R, sigma that gives seconds squared.

prompt: A hiker walks $30\ \mathrm m$ due east, then $0.040\ \mathrm{km}$ in a direction $60^\circ$ north of west, then $2000\ \mathrm{cm}$ due south. Find the magnitude of the net displacement, in m.

rubric.text: Legs converted to metres, then resolved into east and north components
Magnitude from the Pythagorean sum of the totals

solution:
Axes: east $+x$, north $+y$ (vec-comp).
Units: $0.040$ km $=40$ m and $2000$ cm $=20$ m.
Legs: $(30,0)$; $(-40\cos60^\circ,\,40\sin60^\circ)=(-20,\,34.64)$; $(0,-20)$.
$R_x=30-20=10$, $R_y=34.64-20=14.64$ (component sums).
$|R|=\sqrt{10^2+14.64^2}=17.7\ \mathrm m$.
Trap: adding magnitudes gives $90$ m.
hints: Sum x and y separately before taking a magnitude.

prompt: A boat moves at $5.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$ relative to the water. A river $200\ \mathrm m$ wide flows at $3.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$. The boat is steered so that it lands at the point directly opposite its start. The crossing time, in s, is

why: assumed the boat heads straight across, so speed across is 5.0 m/s
used $5.0+3.0=8.0$ m/s across
used the current speed $3.0$ m/s across
used $5.0-3.0=2.0$ m/s across

rubric.text: No net downstream motion imposed: upstream component $=3.0$

solution:
Land opposite: downstream drift must vanish (vec-comp).
Boat velocity relative to water has upstream component $3.0$ m/s.
Its cross-stream component is $\sqrt{5.0^2-3.0^2}=4.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$ (components of a fixed-magnitude vector).
$t=200/4.0=50\ \mathrm s$ (kin-2d: cross and along motions are independent).
hints: Cancel the current with an upstream component; only the rest crosses.

prompt: A constant force $\vec F=(2\hat x+\hat y-3\hat z)\ \mathrm N$ acts on a particle that moves in a straight line from $(1,2,0)\ \mathrm m$ to $(4,-2,3)\ \mathrm m$. Find the work done, in J.

rubric.text: Displacement as final minus initial position
Work written as the dot product $\vec F\cdot\vec d$

solution:
$\vec d=(4-1,\,-2-2,\,3-0)=(3,-4,3)\ \mathrm m$ (vec-comp).
$W=\vec F\cdot\vec d$ (vec-prod: work is a dot product).
$W=2(3)+1(-4)+(-3)(3)=6-4-9=-7\ \mathrm J$.
Negative: the force opposes the net motion.
hints: Work is F dot d, with d = final minus initial position.

prompt: A force $\vec F=(\hat x+3\hat y+2\hat z)\ \mathrm N$ acts at position $\vec r=(2\hat x+\hat y)\ \mathrm m$ from a pivot. The magnitude of the torque about the pivot, in $\mathrm{N\,m}$, is

why: used the dot product $\vec r\cdot\vec F$
used $|r||F|$, assuming the vectors are perpendicular
added the components of $\vec r\times\vec F$ instead of taking the magnitude
forgot the square root of the sum of squares

rubric.text: Torque set up as $\vec\tau=\vec r\times\vec F$
Determinant expansion done with correct signs: $(2,-4,5)$

solution:
$\vec\tau=\vec r\times\vec F$ (vec-prod).
$\tau_x=r_yF_z-r_zF_y=1\cdot2-0=2$.
$\tau_y=r_zF_x-r_xF_z=0-2\cdot2=-4$; $\tau_z=r_xF_y-r_yF_x=6-1=5$.
$|\tau|=\sqrt{4+16+25}=\sqrt{45}=6.7\ \mathrm{N\,m}$ (vec-comp: magnitude from components).
hints: Cross product by determinant, then take the length.

prompt: A car travels at $30\ \mathrm{m/s}$. On its velocity–time graph the speed stays constant for $0.80\ \mathrm s$, then falls linearly, with slope $-5.0\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$, to zero. Find the total distance from $t=0$ to the stop, in m.

rubric.text: Falling section: triangle area $\tfrac12(30)(6.0)=90$ m, or $v^2=2ad$

solution:
Phase 1 (constant speed): $d_1=30(0.80)=24\ \mathrm m$.
Phase 2: $0=v^2-2ad_2$, so $d_2=\dfrac{30^2}{2(5.0)}=90\ \mathrm m$ (kin-1d).
Total $=24+90=114\ \mathrm m$.
Check with a v-t sketch: rectangle $24$ plus triangle $\tfrac12(30)(6.0)=90$ (graphs).
hints: Split the motion into constant speed, then braking.

prompt: On a velocity–time graph, car A is a horizontal line at $20\ \mathrm{m/s}$ and car B is a straight line from the origin with slope $4.0\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. Both cars are at the same point at $t=0$. B catches A at $t=$ (in s)

why: the time when the speeds are equal, not when positions match
dropped the acceleration from $\tfrac12at^2$
halved the acceleration twice: used $\tfrac14at^2$
used $v/(2a)$ for the time

rubric.text: Displacements read as areas under each graph

solution:
Area under A's line: $x_A=20t$ (graphs). Area under B's line: $x_B=\tfrac12(4.0)t^2=2t^2$ (kin-1d).
Catch-up means $x_A=x_B$: $20t=2t^2$.
$t=0$ is the start; the other root is $t=10\ \mathrm s$.
Graph view: B's v-t line reaches $40$ m/s, twice A's speed, and the areas match (graphs).
Trap: equal speeds occur at $t=5$ s, when B is still behind.
hints: Catching up means equal positions, not equal speeds.

prompt: A stone is thrown horizontally at $12\ \mathrm{m/s}$ from the top of a $45\ \mathrm m$ cliff over level ground. Take $g=9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. Find its speed at impact, in m/s.
solution:
Horizontal: $v_x=12\ \mathrm{m/s}$ throughout (kin-2d: independent axes).
Vertical: $v_y^2=2gh=2(9.8)(45)=882$ (kin-1d from rest).
Speed $=\sqrt{12^2+882}=\sqrt{1026}=32.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$ (vec-comp).
Trap: adding $12+29.7=41.7$ treats speeds as collinear.
hints: Energy-free route: vertical fall is plain 1D motion.

prompt: A projectile is launched on level ground with fixed speed. Launch angles $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$ give equal ranges. The ratio of the maximum height at $60^\circ$ to that at $30^\circ$ is

why: used the ratio $\sin60^\circ/\sin30^\circ$, forgetting that $H\propto\sin^2$
assumed equal range means equal height
inverted the ratio
squared the correct ratio again

solution:
Vertical speed at launch: $v\sin\theta$ (kin-2d, components).
At the top $v_y=0$, so $H=\dfrac{v^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}$.
At fixed $v$: $H\propto\sin^2\theta$ (scaling).
$\dfrac{H_{60}}{H_{30}}=\dfrac{(3/4)}{(1/4)}=3$.
hints: Height depends only on the vertical component.

prompt: A velocity-time graph of a cart is piecewise linear. The velocity rises from $0$ to $8\ \mathrm{m/s}$ between $t=0$ and $4\ \mathrm s$, stays at $8\ \mathrm{m/s}$ until $t=10\ \mathrm s$, then falls linearly to $0$ at $t=14\ \mathrm s$. The average velocity over the $14\ \mathrm s$, in m/s, is

why: counted only the rectangle and omitted both triangles
quoted the peak velocity
took the midpoint of the velocity range, $(0+8)/2$
used final minus initial velocity, i.e. mean acceleration

rubric.text: Displacement identified as the area under the v-t graph

solution:
Displacement = area under $v(t)$ (graphs).
Ramp up: $\tfrac12(4)(8)=16$; plateau: $6\times8=48$; ramp down: $\tfrac12(4)(8)=16$.
Total $80\ \mathrm m$ (calc-rates: integral of velocity).
$\bar v=80/14=5.7\ \mathrm{m/s}$ (kin-1d).
hints: Area under v-t is displacement.

prompt: An acceleration-time graph for a cart starting from rest shows $a=3.0\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ constant from $t=0$ to $4.0\ \mathrm s$, then decreasing linearly to $0$ at $t=10\ \mathrm s$. Find the speed at $t=10\ \mathrm s$, in m/s.

rubric.text: Change in speed identified as area under the a-t graph
Triangle $\tfrac12(3.0)(6.0)=9$ added to the start from rest

solution:
$\Delta v=\int a\,dt$ = area under the a-t graph (graphs, calc-rates).
Rectangle $0$ to $4$ s: $3.0\times4.0=12$.
Triangle $4$ to $10$ s: $\tfrac12(6.0)(3.0)=9$.
Start from rest: $v=12+9=21\ \mathrm{m/s}$ (kin-1d).
Trap: using $a_{\max}\times10=30$.
hints: Speed gained is the area under a vs t.

prompt: Estimate the mass of Earth's atmosphere in kg. Use $R_E=6.4\times10^{6}\ \mathrm m$, sea-level pressure $1.0\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{Pa}$ and $g=9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. The closest value is

why: stopped at the weight in newtons, forgot to divide by $g$
multiplied by $g$ instead of dividing
used $R_E$ in kilometres
used the pressure in kPa as if it were in Pa

rubric.text: Atmosphere's weight set equal to pressure times Earth's surface area
Powers of ten tracked in SI

solution:
Weight of the air balances the pressure force: $mg=P\cdot4\pi R_E^2$ (estimate).
$A=4\pi(6.4\times10^6)^2\approx5.1\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{m^2}$.
$m=\dfrac{PA}{g}=\dfrac{(1.0\times10^5)(5.1\times10^{14})}{9.8}\approx5\times10^{18}\ \mathrm{kg}$.
Units: $\mathrm{Pa\,m^2/(m\,s^{-2})}=\mathrm{kg}$ (units, dimanal check).
hints: Pressure times area is the weight of the column.

prompt: Estimate the number of air molecules in a room $8.0\ \mathrm m\times10\ \mathrm m\times3.0\ \mathrm m$. Take $P=1.0\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{Pa}$, $T=300\ \mathrm K$ and $k_B=1.38\times10^{-23}\ \mathrm{J/K}$. The closest value is

why: number density per cubic metre, forgot the volume
used $T=27$ (the Celsius value) instead of kelvin
used a volume of $24\ \mathrm{m^3}$, dropping a factor $10$
used $P=1$ (atm number) with SI $k_BT$

rubric.text: Product $N=nV$ with powers of ten tracked

solution:
$n=\dfrac{P}{k_BT}=\dfrac{1.0\times10^5}{(1.38\times10^{-23})(300)}\approx2.4\times10^{25}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$ (estimate, units).
$V=8.0\times10\times3.0=240\ \mathrm{m^3}$.
$N=nV\approx5.8\times10^{27}\approx6\times10^{27}$ (sigfig: two figures are enough).
Sanity: about $0.4\times10^{4}$ mol, i.e. $10^4$ mol times $6\times10^{23}$ per mol.
hints: N = PV / kT.

prompt: Two solid spheres of the same material and surface finish, with radii $R$ and $2R$, are at the same temperature. Each loses heat at a rate proportional to its surface area. The ratio of the initial cooling rate $|dT/dt|$ of the larger sphere to that of the smaller is

why: inverted the ratio
counted the area ratio only; ignored the larger heat capacity
counted the heat-capacity growth only; ignored the larger area
used the volume ratio

solution:
Heat lost per second $\propto$ area $\propto R^2$ (scaling).
Heat capacity $\propto$ mass $\propto$ volume $\propto R^3$.
$|dT/dt|\propto R^2/R^3=1/R$.
Doubling $R$ halves the rate: $\tfrac12$.
hints: Rate = power out divided by heat capacity.

prompt: The period of small oscillations of a simple pendulum depends only on its length $L$, the acceleration $g$ and its mass. At one site the period is $2.00\ \mathrm s$. At another site $g$ is $2.5$ times larger and the pendulum length is tripled. Find the new period, in s.

rubric.text: Mass excluded and $T\propto\sqrt{L/g}$ established by dimensions
Both factors substituted in the ratio

solution:
Mass cannot appear: only $m$ carries kilograms (dimanal).
$\sqrt{L/g}$ has units of seconds, so $T=k\sqrt{L/g}$ (small-angle: $k$ is a pure number).
Ratio: $T'/T=\sqrt{3/2.5}=1.095$ (scaling).
$T'=2.00\times1.095=2.19\ \mathrm s$.
hints: Dimensions fix T up to a constant; take a ratio.

prompt: In a double-slit experiment the light has wavelength $600\ \mathrm{nm}$, the slit separation is $0.20\ \mathrm{mm}$ and the screen is $2.0\ \mathrm m$ away. The first bright fringe satisfies $d\sin\theta=\lambda$. Using a small-angle approximation, find its distance from the central maximum, in mm.
solution:
$\theta=\lambda/d=\dfrac{6.0\times10^{-7}}{2.0\times10^{-4}}=3.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{rad}$ (small-angle: $\sin\theta\approx\theta$).
$\tan\theta\approx\theta$ at this size, so $y=L\theta$.
$y=2.0\times3.0\times10^{-3}=6.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm m=6.0\ \mathrm{mm}$ (units).
Error from the approximation is below $10^{-5}$ relative.
hints: theta is about 3 milliradians.

prompt: Gravity at height $h$ above Earth's surface is $g(h)=g_0R^2/(R+h)^2$. For a mountain $3.2\ \mathrm{km}$ high, with $R=6.4\times10^{6}\ \mathrm m$, the fractional decrease of $g$ is closest to

why: forgot the factor $2$ in $(1+x)^{-2}\approx1-2x$
used a factor $4$ instead of $2$
slipped a factor $10$ in $h/R$
slipped a factor $10$ the other way in $h/R$

solution:
$g=g_0(1+x)^{-2}$ with $x=h/R=3.2\times10^3/6.4\times10^6=5.0\times10^{-4}$ (units).
$x\ll1$, so $(1+x)^{-2}\approx1-2x$ (small-angle: first-order expansion).
Fractional drop $=2x=1.0\times10^{-3}=0.10\%$ (scaling: relative change doubles with the exponent).
hints: Expand to first order in h/R.

prompt: A car brakes at constant deceleration $\mu g$ after a reaction time $t_r$ at initial speed $v$. A student plots $d/v$ (in s) against $v$ (in m/s) and gets a straight line of slope $0.070\ \mathrm{s^2/m}$ and intercept $0.80\ \mathrm s$, where $d$ is the total stopping distance. Take $g=9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. Find $\mu$.

rubric.text: Divided by $v$ to get the linear form $d/v=t_r+v/(2\mu g)$
Slope equated to $1/(2\mu g)$ and solved

solution:
Model: $d=vt_r+\dfrac{v^2}{2\mu g}$ (kin-1d).
Divide by $v$: $\dfrac dv=t_r+\dfrac{1}{2\mu g}\,v$, a line in $v$ (linearize).
Intercept $=t_r=0.80\ \mathrm s$; slope $=1/(2\mu g)=0.070$ (graphs).
$\mu=\dfrac{1}{2(9.8)(0.070)}=0.729$.
Trap: dropping the 2 gives $1.46$.
hints: Divide the stopping-distance law by v.

prompt: For two moons of one planet, a log-log plot of orbital period against orbital radius is a straight line. Moon 1 has $r=2.0\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{km}$ and $T=1.0$ day. Moon 2 has $r=8.0\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{km}$ and $T=8.0$ days. The period at $r=4.0\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{km}$, in days, is closest to

why: assumed $T\propto r$
assumed $T\propto r^2$
interpolated linearly on a $T$ versus $r$ plot
took the mean of $1.0$ and $8.0$

rubric.text: Straight log-log line means a power law $T=kr^n$

solution:
Straight on log-log axes means $T=kr^n$ (linearize: $\ln T=n\ln r+\ln k$).
$n=\dfrac{\ln(8.0/1.0)}{\ln(8.0/2.0)}=\dfrac{\ln 8}{\ln 4}=1.5$ (graphs: slope).
$r$ doubles from Moon 1, so $T=1.0\times2^{1.5}=2.8$ days (scaling).
Trap: linear interpolation on $T$ versus $r$ gives $3.3$.
hints: Slope on log-log axes is the exponent.

prompt: A particle moves along a line with $x(t)=2t^3-9t^2+12t$, with $x$ in m and $t$ in s. Find the total distance travelled from $t=0$ to $t=3\ \mathrm s$, in m.

rubric.text: Distances summed over each leg with absolute values

solution:
$v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}=6t^2-18t+12=6(t-1)(t-2)$ (calc-rates).
The particle reverses at $t=1$ and $t=2$ (graphs: $v$ changes sign).
$x(0)=0$, $x(1)=5$, $x(2)=4$, $x(3)=9$ (kin-1d).
Distance $=5+1+5=11\ \mathrm m$; net displacement is only $9$ m.
hints: Distance is not displacement: find where v changes sign.

prompt: A current $I(t)=I_0\sin(\omega t)$ flows in a wire from $t=0$ to $t=\pi/\omega$, one half period. The charge that passes a cross section in that interval is

why: used peak current times duration
evaluated $1-\cos(\pi)$ as $1$
wrong dimensions: $\omega$ in the numerator, not charge
integrated over a full period instead of a half period

rubric.text: Antiderivative $-\tfrac{I_0}{\omega}\cos\omega t$ evaluated at the limits

solution:
$I=dQ/dt$, so $Q=\int_0^{\pi/\omega}I\,dt$ (calc-rates).
$Q=-\dfrac{I_0}{\omega}\cos\omega t\Big|_0^{\pi/\omega}=\dfrac{I_0}{\omega}\,(1-\cos\pi)=\dfrac{2I_0}{\omega}$.
Units: $\mathrm A/(\mathrm{s^{-1}})=\mathrm{A\,s}=\mathrm C$ (dimanal).
Graph check: area under one arch of a sine is $2\times$ peak $\times\,\omega^{-1}$ (graphs).
hints: Charge is the time integral of current.
